articles.standfirst: La información que compartía RTVE señalaba que el Presidente del Gobierno empleará el fin de semana para dirimir cuáles serán los siguientes pasos a seguir
articles.summary: La información que compartía RTVE señalaba que el Presidente del Gobierno empleará el fin de semana para dirimir cuáles serán los siguientes pasos a seguir
articles.body: Pedro Sánchez se marchaba rápidamente del Congreso de los Diputados tras las dos votaciones fallidas por ambos real decreto ley que trataban de paliar la crisis que atraviesa España en materia de vivienda. Una imagen que se unía a una noticia que ha estado en el debate público desde primera hora de la mañana donde se afirmaba que podría haber un adelanto electoral para el próximo 29 de noviembre de 2026. Pues bien, según una información de RTVE que han compartido en el especial desde el Congreso de los Diputados, el presidente del Gobierno se enfrenta a un "periodo de reflexión" y decidirá si convoca elecciones durante este fin de semana. Por lo que la decisión sobre un adelanto electoral deberá de esperar. La posibilidad de un adelanto de las elecciones generales ha cobrado fuerza ante el rechazo este viernes en el Congreso de los Diputados de los dos decretos sobre vivienda aprobados por el Consejo de Ministros. El rechazo anunciado por Junts, sumado a la oposición de PP, Vox y UPN, ha elevado la presión sobre Pedro Sánchez. El presidente del Gobierno ha insistido hasta ahora en que las elecciones generales se celebrarán en 2027. Sin embargo, algunas fuentes citadas en el entorno político consideran que el rechazo de los decretos podría modificar ese escenario y abrir la puerta a una convocatoria anticipada. Una información que corresponde exclusivamente a Sánchez y que, según las citadas fuentes de la cadena pública, estaría en un "periodo de reflexión" para tomar una decisión final. Ha sido el líder de la oposición, Alberto Núñez Feijoó, tras el momento en el que el Congreso de los Diputados ha declinado los dos decretos, cuando ha salido ha hablar públicamente con los medios de comunicación que estaban presentes en el emiciclo y cuando ha vuelto a solicitar un adelanto electoral argumentando que tras esta votación el Gobierno ya no puede seguir con sus funciones: "Ponga la fecha, disuelva las cortes, convoque elecciones, que hablen los españoles".

articles.title: Fact check: Trump’s attempt to pretend he didn’t say the Iran war would last mere ‘weeks’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has a long history of trying to rewrite history about his own public remarks. He is now doing it again about the war with Iran – wrong...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has a long history of trying to rewrite history about his own public remarks. He is now doing it again about the war with Iran – wrongly describing his own past predictions that the war would last mere weeks.

In March, Trump said he thought the war he launched on the last day of February would be over in "four weeks," "four to five weeks," "four to six weeks," or otherwise under two months. But in a social media post on Thursday, a full seven months after the war began, he claimed that his "four to six weeks" projections had just been about the time it would take to eradicate the nuclear threat from Iran – in other words, not the time it would take to conclude the entire war.

"I stated, numerous times, that it would take 4-6 weeks to get rid of THE IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, and I did it in one night! The rest of the time is just to make sure it stays that way," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

And when a journalist from TIME Magazine reminded Trump in a Monday interview published earlier Thursday that "I feel like most people heard you say four to six weeks," Trump responded, "No, I think the press fed it to them."

No. That's indeed what Trump said. So did his White House press secretary – citing Trump's own words.

In this article, we will mostly leave aside Trump's Thursday assertion that he eliminated the nuclear threat from Iran in the first day of the war, which is rejected by many experts. We'll focus on his inaccurate depiction of his own prior comments about the length of the conflict.

Trump and his press secretary repeatedly said the war would last just weeks

It's possible that Trump said somewhere at some point that he was referring specifically to the nuclear threat when he spoke of being finished in weeks. But the White House couldn't provide any examples when CNN asked if there were any, instead emailing a reply on Friday morning that declared Trump "right" but didn't address our specific request for proof.

Even if some examples do exist, Trump clearly said in multiple public comments that he thought the entire war would be finished in just weeks. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt echoed those claims, regularly using a timeline of "four to six weeks" and attributing it to Trump. Here is a sampling of what they said.

March 2, Trump interview with CNN: Less than three days into the war, CNN anchor Jake Tapper asked Trump in an interview how long the war might last. Trump responded , "I don't want to see it go on too long. I always thought it would be four weeks. And we're a little ahead of schedule."

March 2, Trump speech: In a speech later that day, Trump made a projection of "four to five weeks" while talking about the war as a whole, though he left the door open to a longer conflict: "We have the strongest and most powerful, by far, military in the world, and we will easily prevail. We're already substantially ahead of our time projections. But whatever the time is, it's OK. Whatever it takes, we will always – and we have, right from the beginning, we projected four to five weeks, but we have capability to go far longer than that."

March 10, Leavitt briefing: Asked about the current timeline for how long the war would last, Leavitt repeated that "four to six weeks" was the initial timeline for achieving all the objectives of the war – not just addressing a nuclear threat from Iran.

"The president and the US military's initial timeline was about four to six weeks to achieve the full objectives of Operation Epic Fury," she said. "Again, to destroy their missiles and their ability to make them, destroy their navy, permanently deny them nuclear weapons forever and to, of course, weaken their evil terrorist proxies in the region." She added that the military was "well ahead of schedule" but that Trump would ultimately decide when the objectives had been met.

March 25, Leavitt briefing: Leavitt cited an estimate of "approximately four to six weeks" for the war as a whole, again claiming the military was ahead of schedule: "From the outset, President Trump and the Department of War estimated it would take approximately four to six weeks to achieve this critical mission. Twenty-five days in, the greatest military the world has ever known is ahead of schedule and performing exceptionally."

March 26, Trump remarks at Cabinet meeting: Trump twice repeated a "four to six weeks" estimate while talking about the war as a whole, and he said both times that the US was ahead of this schedule.

First, he said, "We estimated it would take approximately four to six weeks to achieve our mission, and we're way ahead of schedule. If you look at what we've done in terms of the destruction of that country, I mean we're way ahead. Think of it: they have no navy, and they had good ships; 154 ships have been shot down and are resting very nicely at the bottom of the sea."

Second, he said: "And we did that in a matter of less than a week, because we have the greatest military in the world by far, nobody even close. So we estimated it would take approximately four to six weeks to achieve our mission; 26 days in, we're extremely – really a lot ahead of schedule. The Iranian regime is now admitting to itself that they have been decisively defeated."

March 30, Leavitt briefing: Leavitt told reporters , "With respect to the timeline, again, the president, commander-in-chief, the Pentagon has always stated four to six weeks estimated timeline for Operation Epic Fury."

March 31, Trump exchange with reporters: Talking about the war, Trump said , "I would say that within two weeks, maybe; two weeks, maybe three." When a reporter asked if he meant "the US will be gone or done with the war in two weeks," Trump said, "I think two or three weeks, yeah." And when a reporter began a follow-up question by saying "that three weeks, if it is…" Trump interjected and said, "We'll leave."

A bit later, the president said, "I had one goal, they will have no nuclear weapon, and that goal has been attained. They will not have nuclear weapons. But we're finishing the job. And I think within maybe two weeks, maybe a couple of days longer, to do the job, but we want to knock out every single thing they have."

In other words, though he referred to the Iranian nuclear threat, he explicitly said he thought the US would be done with the war less than eight weeks after it started.

April 8, Leavitt briefing: Leavitt said , "From the very beginning of Operation Epic Fury, President Trump stated this would be a four-to-six-week military operation to dismantle the military threat posed by the radical Islamic Iranian regime. Thanks to the unbelievable capabilities of America's warfighters, the United States has achieved and exceeded those core military objectives in just 38 days."

Trump and his administration made various vaguer comments

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was frequently less specific than Trump on the expected length of the war. On March 2, the day Trump said "four weeks" and then "four to five weeks," Hegseth said , "President Trump has all the latitude in the world to talk about how long it may or may not take four weeks, two weeks, six weeks. It could move up, it could move back."

And at various times, including in March, Trump offered vaguer comments on how long the war would last – for example, saying March 9 that it would end "very soon" without providing a timeline. In a social media post in April, he was already distancing himself from his prior estimates of six weeks or less, claiming it was Democrats who "like to say that I promised 6 weeks to defeat Iran."

He can quibble about whether he made a promise or offered an estimate. But the record shows the "six weeks" figure came from his own mouth.

articles.title: Feijóo exige elecciones a Sánchez tras el rechazo en los decretos de vivienda: “Ha preferido fracasar dos veces”
articles.standfirst: Previstas para el 2027, el ‘no’ del Congreso abre la puerta a unos posibles comicios
articles.summary: Previstas para el 2027, el ‘no’ del Congreso abre la puerta a unos posibles comicios
articles.body: Este viernes, 2 de octubre, los votos en contra de PP, Vox y Junts han tumbado los dos decretos de vivienda presentados por el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, tras el desahucio de Maricarmen. Algo que sus rivales políticos han usado para exigir la convocatoria de elecciones anticipadas. Uno de los primeros en pronunciarse ha sido Alberto Núñez Feijóo, líder del Partido Popular. El político gallego ha sido muy duro con Sánchez: “Han presentado dos decretos incompatibles entre sí, defendidos al mismo tiempo por distintas partes del Gobierno. Lo han hecho remitiéndolos a la Cámara de madrugada y enviándolos sin haber sido aprobados previamente por el Consejo de Ministros”, comenzó diciendo, denunciando las formas en las que se han intentado aprobar estas dos normativas. “Lo han hecho, además, con publicaciones diferenciadas en el Boletín Oficial del Estado sobre un mismo asunto. Y, como acabamos de ver, lo han hecho sin contar con la mayoría de la Cámara. A la vez, han preferido fracasar dos veces”, prosiguió. Tildando como “fracaso” el ejecutivo actual, apuntando a las elecciones: “El tamaño de la derrota del Gobierno solo es comparable con la frivolidad imperdonable con la que han tratado el asunto más relevante de los últimos años para la ciudadanía española: la vivienda”. Pasando, entonces, a hablar para el común de la sociedad: “Por eso, en primer lugar, quiero dirigirme a los españoles preocupados por el resultado de este debate; a todas las personas vulnerables que saben que iban a verse perjudicadas porque tendrían más dificultades para alquilar; a los más de tres millones y medio de propietarios que tienen una vivienda alquilada y, sobre todo, a los jóvenes que estaban esperando poder alquilar una vivienda a un precio asequible o incluso poder comprarla a través de un préstamo”. “A todos ellos podemos decirles que el resultado de las votaciones de hoy, al menos, garantiza que la situación de la vivienda no esté peor que ayer. Eso no significa que vaya a estar mejor mañana. Lamentablemente, no será así hasta que en este país se adopten las medidas adecuadas”, denunció. Postulándose para dirigir el cambio de gobierno: "Hay una alternativa creíble. Han intentado hacer creer a la gente que es responsabilidad de la oposición. Es impresentable usar la vivienda para maniobras electorales”. “Hoy no se ha votado un decreto para ayudar a Maricarmen ni a nadie, aquí se ha traído una excusa para ayudar a Pedro Sánchez. Que convoque elecciones y no guarde mucho más la fecha, estamos preparados. Las únicas salidas decentes y democráticas son la convocatoria de elecciones", sentenció.

articles.title: Kennedy Center Honors to be held off-site for the first time in the ceremony’s history
articles.summary: For the first time in the nearly 50-year history of the event, the Kennedy Center Honors will not be held inside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts this year, the center announced Friday.
articles.body: For the first time in the nearly 50-year history of the event, the Kennedy Center Honors will not be held inside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts this year, the center announced Friday. With the main building currently closed to the public, and safety assessments still underway, the center announced it plans to move the celebration of American performing arts to Capital One Arena in downtown Washington, D.C., which seats around 20,000 people compared to the 2,300 seats in the center’s Opera House, where the awards ceremony has traditionally been held. This year’s ceremony is scheduled for Dec. 7. The center says they will announce this year’s honorees at a later date. Even the 2020 Kennedy Center Honors, held belatedly in May of 2021 due to the Coronavirus pandemic, included performances that were taped over several days at various locations throughout the Kennedy Center’s campus. The change of venue for the storied event comes as the main theaters at the Kennedy Center have been closed since Sept. 15, after the center’s board voted to close for renovations. In court filings, Executive Director Matt Floca explained the closure would be reconsidered on a week-by-week basis, depending on the status of ongoing safety assessment. The Kennedy Center’s board had cited a partial ceiling collapse in the center’s Grand Foyer last month as evidence that the center needed to be immediately closed for repairs. A construction consultant and the center’s director “consider the main building to be unsafe for continued occupancy, and anticipate further risk to the public and employees if the building is not immediately closed and renovations begun,” the board said in a draft resolution to close the center for two years during the planned construction. But President Donald Trump has previously said renovations wouldn’t happen — and the building could potentially even be demolished — unless his name was added to the building — something a federal judge has blocked multiple times as litigation over the closure and effort to rename the center proceeds. “The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in September. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.” The White House declined to comment to NBC News about the change in venue for the annual awards ceremony.

articles.title: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name
articles.body:
This year's Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington's Capital One Arena, not the riverfront building that's been at the center of a legal fight over adding President Donald Trump's name to the building.

The 49th annual awards are set to take place at Washington's downtown arena, a Kennedy Center spokesperson said Friday. Few other details were immediately available, and an explanation for the change wasn't given.

The center's board voted last month to close the iconic performing arts venue along the Potomac River waterfront after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building.

Trump has said in social media posts that the center needed to close for safety repairs . But he said the repairs would only happen if the board was allowed to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.

A federal judge has twice said that can't happen without the approval of Congress, which has allocated $257 million for repairs.

The president hosted the 2025 awards , whose honorees included Sylvester Stallone and George Strait. He said at the time that he would rename the facility the "Trump Kennedy Center," and not long after workers began adding his name to the building.

The board of trustees, named by Trump, voted unanimously for the change , which has been challenged in court since.

Congress named the performing arts center as a living memorial to John F. Kennedy in 1964, the year after he was assassinated.

The law explicitly prohibits the board of trustees from making the center into a memorial to anyone else, and from putting another person's name on the building's exterior.

The Kennedy Center Honors, which recognize people for lifetime contributions to American culture through the performing arts, was established in 1978. The 2026 honorees are set to be named at a later day, the center's spokesperson said. The event will take place on Dec. 7.

articles.title: FBI gives employees a classified 'Patel Report' about times when it 'fell short'
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI has released a classified report to its workforce examining what it says are chapters from the bureau's history "where this institution fell short," according to an internal message obtained Friday by The Associated Press.

It was unclear what episodes from the FBI's past are chronicled in the new "Patel Report." But the document's existence is in keeping with Director Kash Patel's frequent criticism of the leaders who preceded him as well as with his determination to rid the FBI of agents and other employees he contends have politicized the bureau in the past. Patel's critics, however, accuse him of politicizing the FBI.

Though Patel pledged at his confirmation hearing last year that he would not look "backward," he has encouraged investigation of former senior officials and has presided over waves of terminations, including of employees who participated in years-old investigations of President Donald Trump, were photographed taking a knee during a 2020 racial justice protest and contributed to a disputed analytical memo about Catholic extremism.

"The Patel Report looks backward because accountability demands it," says a memo to the workforce signed by the FBI's co-deputy directors, Christopher Raia and Andrew Bailey, that describes the document as marking the "closing of one chapter in our history and the beginning of another complete with a brighter future ahead."

Bailey announced his resignation earlier this week, and his last day is Friday. The FBI declined to comment on the report.

The message also says: "We cannot change what happened before we arrived. But we can confront it honestly. We can recognize failures instead of protecting them. We can hold people accountable. We can fix what was broken. And we can build safeguards strong enough to ensure the mistakes of the past are never allowed to define this institution again. These steps are consistent with any institution of excellence that is constantly striving for improvement."

It was unclear if the report made recommendations or demanded any action to address past shortcomings.

The FBI message says the report is meant to "promote fierce organizational accountability" and rebuild "public trust."

But Patel's critics say the politically charged investigations into perceived adversaries of Trump that the FBI has started under his watch, as well as the punishment of agents who participated in investigations into the Republican president to which they were assigned, have eroded faith in the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency.

articles.title: LePage breaks with Trump on Iran, Canada tariffs, immigration in Maine House debate
articles.summary: Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R) split with the Trump administration on key issues — including the Iran war, tariffs and immigration — during a Thursday debate in the open U.S. House race in the state’s 2nd Congressional District. LePage, the GOP nominee, who is running against Matt Dunlap (D), the state auditor, previously criticized…
articles.body:
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R) split with the Trump administration on key issues — including the Iran war, tariffs and immigration — during a Thursday debate in the open U.S. House race in the state’s 2nd Congressional District.

LePage, the GOP nominee, who is running against Matt Dunlap (D), the state auditor, previously criticized the administration’s widespread immigration crackdown efforts after he said his son’s father-in-law was being wrongfully deported .

During the Thursday debate hosted by local outlet WMTW, LePage called for increased accountability and transparency from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement around its deportation operations.

Additionally, the Republican nominee expressed disagreement with the Trump administration’s tariffs on Canada and leaned on his experience facilitating negotiations over the North American Free Trade Agreement under the first Trump administration.

“We need to de-escalate the rhetoric, and we need to get the president and the prime minister of Canada back to the negotiating table,” LePage said.

Despite disagreeing with the Trump administration in segments of the debate, LePage also touted his past experience working with the president during his time as governor.

“I know him personally, and I will say right now, I will be able to get into the Oval Office,” LePage said, adding, “My opponent will not.”

The GOP candidate urged President Trump to bring the ongoing Iran war to a close “as quick as possible,” but he said he would oppose a war powers resolution if elected. The House has passed three Iran war powers resolutions with the support of several Republican lawmakers.

Dunlap criticized LePage’s response to a war powers resolution question, pointing to rising energy prices tied to the ongoing conflict.

“Your heating oil is $7 a gallon because of the Iran war. Paul LePage can’t decide if he’s for it or against it,” Dunlap wrote in a social media post after the debate.

LePage and Dunlap will face off again in a second debate on Oct. 15.

Republicans are hoping to flip this key swing district in November, which is currently represented by retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden. Trump won the district by 9 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates the race as “Likely Republican.” However, recent polling has shown Dunlap leading the former governor among likely voters.

In a University of New Hampshire survey released at the end of September, the Democrat had a 6-point advantage over his GOP opponent.

articles.title: Kansas Democratic Senate nominee says ‘please, no’ to Harris campaigning for him
articles.summary: Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton said “please, no” on Thursday to the possibility of former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning with him ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Appearing on Politico’s “The Conversation,” Hamilton discussed which national Democrats he would be willing to campaign with. “It wasn’t like I was a huge champion for…
articles.body:
Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton said “please, no” on Thursday to the possibility of former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning with him ahead of the 2026 midterm elections .

Appearing on Politico’s “ The Conversation ,” Hamilton discussed which national Democrats he would be willing to campaign with.

“It wasn’t like I was a huge champion for Kamala Harris,” he said. “People ask me, should she come here and campaign for you? Please, no. Don’t come here to campaign for me.”

“Harris can stay in California. Yeah, and I mean no disrespect for her. I just think she is not somebody who would win votes here in Kansas,” Hamilton added.

While he has campaigned with Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Hamilton similarly declined the opportunity to campaign with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

He then recounted Schumer asking him what would be the biggest challenge in the Kansas Senate race.

“I said, ‘You, you know, you are,’” he continued. “I am only saying in Kansas, you’re a liability. You’re not a, you’re not a help.”

Harris has campaigned with other Democratic candidates in battleground states, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

“Remember, the Senate seat is six years. So let’s think about that in the lives of all the people that the leaders here serve,” Harris said alongside El-Sayed at a discussion on Black maternal healthcare.

Her involvement in Democratic campaigns in traditionally red states has divided the party , with former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) Senate campaign distancing itself from the former vice president.

“The VP did very well in some places and didn’t do great in others, and if you’re in a state where she didn’t perform well, it may not help you to have her campaign with you this fall,” Democratic strategist and former Harris aide Jamal Simmons told The Hill in August.

President Trump won Kansas in 2024 by nearly 16 points over Harris, but his approval rating in the Sunflower State has slipped to around 40 percent, according to a September Emerson College and Nexstar poll .

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) is the favorite to win his race against Hamilton, but the generally bad political atmosphere for Republicans could open a window for the Democrat.

The Emerson poll also found Hamilton slightly ahead of Marshall at 45 percent support to the Republican’s 43 percent.

Kansas is generally a red state, and, although it has sometimes elected moderate Democratic governors, it has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932.

articles.title: Former GOP Rep. David Rivera sentenced to 10 years for secret Venezuela lobbying
articles.summary: The trial included testimony from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a former roommate and longtime friend of Rivera.
articles.body: MIAMI — A former Miami congressman and longtime friend of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was sentenced Friday to 10 years in prison in connection with a secret $50 million lobbying campaign on Venezuela’s behalf during the first Trump administration. Republican David Rivera has been jailed since jurors found him guilty in May on all counts, including failing to register as a foreign agent and conspiracy to commit money laundering as part of his work for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro ’s government. Rivera, 61, appeared stone-faced as Judge Melissa Damian denounced him for betraying his life’s mission, saying he would surely have been judged harshly his many friends had the millions of dollars come from the Cuban regime instead of its allies in Caracas. “Nobody would accept that’s OK and I don’t think this is different,” the judge said. “There’s no dispute this money came from the Maduro regime.” The seven-week trial offered a rare glimpse into Miami’s role as a crossroads for foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping U.S. policy toward Latin America, highlighting the city’s reputation as a magnet for both anti-communist crusaders and corruption among its sizable exile population. It included testimony from President Donald Trump’s secretary of state, Rep. Pete Sessions of Texas and a top Washington lobbyist — all of whom testified they felt betrayed when learning of Rivera’s mammoth consulting contract with a U.S.-based affiliate of Venezuela’s state oil company, PDVSA. Attorneys for Rivera plan to appeal and in June applied for a presidential pardon. Rivera faces additional federal charges in Washington, D.C., in a related foreign lobbying case. Prosecutors said betrayal featured coded figures In an indictment unsealed in 2022, prosecutors alleged that Rivera was tapped by then Foreign Minister Delcy Rodríguez — now Venezuela’s acting president — to work Republican connections to get the first Trump administration to abandon its hard line and crippling sanctions on Venezuela. As part of the charm offensive, Rivera and a co-defendant, political consultant Esther Nuhfer, sought to manipulate influential friends, including Rubio and Sessions. Their goal was to normalize relations with the new Trump administration even as the Maduro government faced sanctions over serious accusations of human rights violations. But Rivera and Nuhfer didn’t disclose their lobbying work as required, for fear it would have ended Rivera’s political career as an anti-communist stalwart, prosecutors argued at trial. “The United States and the public were the true victims of this fraud,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Roger Cruz said in urging a stiff sentence. “He used his position of trust — and betrayed it consistently and repeatedly.” To hide his work, prosecutors allege, Rivera also set up an encrypted chat group called MIA — for Miami — with his main conduit to the Maduro government: Venezuelan media tycoon Raúl Gorrín, who was subsequently charged in the U.S. with bribing top Venezuelan officials. Members of the group used playful code words to discuss their activities: Maduro was the “bus driver,” Sessions “Sombrero,” Rodríguez “The Lady in Red,” and their windfall payments “La Luz,” Spanish for “The Light,” according to copies of text messages presented to the jury. Rubio was known as “Miss Clairol,” because rubio means blond in Spanish. $50 million contract and missing paperwork At Friday’s sentencing, attorneys for Rivera repeated their trial argument that the former congressman believed he was under no requirement to disclose the work. The three-month, $50 million contract with Rivera’s one-man consulting firm, they said, was focused on luring oil giant ExxonMobil back to Venezuela — commercial work that is generally exempt from the Foreign Agents Registration Act. “David Rivera does not deserve to die in prison because he failed to file a FARA registration,” defense attorney Ed Shohat said at Friday’s hearing. “If he had filed that paper, that form, everything he did, including the $50 million contract, which totally distorted this case, is perfectly legal.” Wholly distinct from that consulting work, they say, were Rivera’s meetings with Rubio and Sessions, which were focused on ushering in leadership in Venezuela that would be less hostile to the U.S. — not supporting Maduro in normalizing relations with the U.S. “There’s not one word in any chat, not one document, not one thing he did to help Nicolás Maduro,” said Shohat. Prosecutors said Rivera used the contract with the affiliate, New York-based PDV USA, as cover for illegal lobbying. “This is a classic money laundering case,” the judge said Friday in rejecting Rivera’s motion to lower the federal guidelines range. Where did the money go? The partners tried to hide the work — backdating documents and coming up with sham agreements, like one to justify a wire transfer of $3.75 million to a South Florida company that maintained Gorrín’s luxury yacht, prosecutors said. The political activity included setting up meetings for Rodríguez in New York, Caracas, Washington and Dallas. As part of the effort, Rivera roped in Sessions, who later tried to broker a meeting for Rodríguez with the ExxonMobil executive who took over as CEO when Rex Tillerson became Trump’s first-term secretary of state. After a secret meeting in Caracas with Maduro, Sessions also agreed to deliver a letter from the Venezuelan president to Trump. The outreach quickly unraveled, however. Within six months of taking office, Trump sanctioned Maduro and labeled him a “dictator,” launching a “maximum pressure” campaign to unseat the president. And now, nearly a decade later, Rodríguez has emerged as the second Trump administration’s trusted partner after the U.S. military’s ousting of Maduro. Rubio’s former housemate faced scandal before Before being elected to Congress in 2010, Rivera was a high-ranking Florida legislator and shared a Tallahassee home with Rubio, who eventually became the Florida House speaker. Rivera faced earlier controversy, including allegations that he secretly funded a Democratic spoiler candidate in a 2012 congressional race. Last year, federal prosecutors dropped that case after an appeals court threw out a sizable fine imposed by a lower court. Rivera was also investigated — but never charged — for alleged campaign finance violations and a $1 million contract with a gambling company while serving in the Florida Legislature. Despite all that, Rivera remains popular among Miami’s Cuban American establishment. Friends of the former congressman, including the former president of Florida International University and Miami-Dade County’s supervisor of elections, packed the courtroom to show their support. Sessions, in a letter seeking leniency that was read into the record by his chief of staff, said his former congressional colleague devoted decades to public service, much of it focused on defending liberty and democracy. “I don’t think it’s productive for society by sending David away for a long, long time,” testified Liliana Ros, a longtime Miami GOP committee member.

articles.title: Trump: Cornell students ‘won’t get a fair shake’ with James leading probe
articles.summary: President Trump criticized the appointment of New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) as a special prosecutor investigating the Cornell University rape case, arguing people “won’t get a fair shake” with her in the role. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed James to the case. James previously investigated and sued Trump, and the two…
articles.body:
President Trump criticized the appointment of New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) as a special prosecutor investigating the Cornell University rape case, arguing people “won’t get a fair shake” with her in the role.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed James to the case. James previously investigated and sued Trump, and the two have repeatedly battled in public.

“Letitia James is a corrupt person,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn en route to Alabama on Friday.

“I feel bad for whoever she’s looking at because they won’t get a fair shake,” he added.

The president and New York attorney general have a long-running feud, which has included state lawsuits against the administration’s policies and her move to sue the Trump administration over fraud.

Trump’s comments came hours after Hochul tapped James for the role. Hochul said she lacked confidence in the district attorney to handle the matter.

“I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law. In the coming months, my office will dutifully carry out the responsibilities the governor has conferred upon us in this executive order. We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions,” James said at a Friday press conference alongside Hochul.

The developments are the latest in the investigation into an alleged gang rape at a campus fraternity in 2025.

A woman who was a sophomore at Cornell at the time of the incident has sued the university, the fraternity, her own sorority and seven men she says were involved in assaulting her.

A local district attorney declined to bring charges after reviewing the matter. According to a report by The New York Times , some of the men named in the lawsuit acknowledged sexual contact with the woman but said it had been consensual.

articles.title: Thousands of immigrants with legal status lose Medicaid coverage as ‘big, beautiful’ cuts begin
articles.summary: Thousands of refugees and some other immigrants with legal status lost their health coverage Oct. 1, marking some of the first significant coverage losses under the Medicaid cuts in the GOP’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. States and advocacy groups have been trying to warn immigrants who were previously eligible for Medicaid — such…
articles.body:
Thousands of refugees and some other immigrants with legal status lost their health coverage Oct. 1, marking some of the first significant coverage losses under the Medicaid cuts in the GOP’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

States and advocacy groups have been trying to warn immigrants who were previously eligible for Medicaid — such as refugees, asylees without a green card, survivors of domestic violence and victims of sex trafficking — that they no longer qualify.

“This is a real shift that’s going to create a serious gap in access to healthcare services,” said Adriana Cadena, executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition. “The folks who have survived the most trauma, whether it’s war, natural disaster, or sexual assault, are going to be the folks who are going to be losing coverage.”

Advocates say the eligibility restrictions on immigrants will mean people lose access to doctors, as well as medications and treatments for diabetes and other chronic diseases.

Providers will lose longtime patients, and hospitals expect a spike in uninsured emergency room visits, which could drive up health system costs. Hospitals are required to provide emergency care regardless of immigration status and are reimbursed by Emergency Medicaid.

The law does not impact green card holders or a few other small groups of immigrants. The law also doesn’t change existing state options to cover children and pregnant immigrants; states can still receive federal matching funding for these populations.

The Medicaid eligibility restrictions are merely the first in a host of provisions that are projected to strip away government-sponsored health coverage.

Starting next year, more than 1 million immigrants are projected to lose Affordable Care Act plan subsidies as well as Medicare coverage.

The changes are part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, President Trump and congressional Republicans’ signature domestic policy legislation that he signed into law with much fanfare in 2025. The law is projected to cut Medicaid spending by $900 billion through 2034, largely by imposing new eligibility restrictions, work requirements and cost sharing.

In selling the bill to Congress, the administration argued that “illegal aliens” would be losing Medicaid.

“The One, Big, Beautiful Bill is a generational chance to protect Medicaid for Americans by removing at least 1.4 million illegal immigrants from the program,” the White House said in a May 2025 statement.

But immigrants without legal status are already ineligible for federally funded health coverage.

The law also imposed restrictions on immigrants’ use of food stamps, Medicare and the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that the Medicaid changes would lead to roughly 100,000 lawfully present immigrants losing health insurance.

Immigrant advocates said the actual number could be significantly higher because of the Trump administration’s slowing of green-card applications; many immigrants with legal status will be kicked off Medicaid while they wait for their application decisions.

According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, it takes an average of 30 months to process an application for permanent residence from a refugee who was admitted more than a year ago.

Ben D’Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, said it was “shocking” to see Republicans try to demonize immigrants who had been admitted to the country for humanitarian reasons.

“These are people who are among the most vulnerable and among the most vetted categories of immigrants,” D’Avanzo said.

Federal officials said the law ensures U.S. government money is spent on Americans and forces immigrants to be self-sufficient.

“Immigrants must be able to support themselves and not depend on benefits paid for by hard-working American taxpayers. President Trump and this administration will always put American citizens first,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement.

Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank focused on lower immigration rates, said he supports the administration’s attempt to curtail immigrants’ use of welfare programs.

But he said the savings from restricting immigrants from Medicaid would be fairly modest. Much bigger savings would result from overhauling the entire immigration system.

“If we really want legal immigrants to use less welfare we would need to have a system that selects future immigrants based on skills who are unlikely to need welfare,” Camarota said.

Advocates said many of the people losing coverage will be forced to turn to emergency rooms for care, seeking treatment only when they get extremely ill or injured.

D’Avanzo said it’s a false premise that cutting immigrants off from Medicaid saves money, because the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become Medicaid-eligible green card holders.

“But in the meantime, they will put off preventative care. They will have sacrificed medication that controls chronic conditions. They will not have sought treatment for their diabetes or their heart disease,” D’Avanzo said. “And by the time they become Medicaid-eligible again, they will have conditions that have not been treated because they could not afford to, and instead we’ll be seeing people in the emergency room.”

Some states and advocacy groups have been working to find alternatives to Medicaid coverage, but there aren’t many available.

People could pay out of pocket at Federally Qualified Health Centers, which provide primary and preventive care regardless of immigration status and offer sliding-scale fees based on income.

Immigrants can also purchase an Affordable Care Act (ACA) plan, but the costs are often a barrier. Congressional Republicans allowed the law’s enhanced premium subsidies to expire last year, and the same group of immigrants who are now ineligible for Medicaid will also become ineligible for regularly subsidized ACA plans on Jan. 1.

Shanteny Jackson, executive director of the Virginia Community Health Worker Association, said there are about 6,000 lawfully present immigrants in her state who lost Medicaid coverage.

Some may be eligible to enroll in a new program through the state’s ACA exchange, which helps lower people’s premiums on top of any federal tax credits.

But eligibility is limited to people with household incomes between 138 percent and 250 percent of the federal poverty level — between $22,025 and $39,900 for an individual or $45,540 and $82,500 for a family of four.

Cadena, of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, said she worries about mixed-status households and the trickle-down impact on U.S. citizen children.

“Children are more likely to get care when their parents have care,” Cadena said. “So if parents are losing access to this care, then they would assume, or could believe, that the child is also losing access,” even though the child would remain eligible as a U.S. citizen.

“A quarter of all children in the United States live in immigrant families. So we could be talking about some very big numbers when we take all of this into account,” Cadena added.

images.caption: Thousands of refugees and other legal immigrants are set to lose their health coverage today, as key provisions slashing Medicaid in the GOP’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act take effect.

articles.title: Karine Jean-Pierre admits Biden admin failed on economic, age messaging, but claims Trump making same mistake
articles.summary: Karine Jean-Pierre argued President Donald Trump is repeating former President Joe Biden's messaging failures on the economy, warning that grocery and gas prices remain undefeated.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre argued in an opinion piece published Friday that President Donald Trump was making the same messaging mistakes as her former boss, former President Joe Biden. "Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda," she wrote in The New York Times guest essay. "His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land. "Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation." FOX NEWS POLL: AS ECONOMIC PAIN DEEPENS, DISAPPROVAL OF TRUMP HITS NEW HIGH Jean-Pierre pointed to the president's messaging on gas prices, inflation and the war in Iran in the piece and said, "When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses." "The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging," she wrote. When asked about Jean-Pierre's argument, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Biden’s policies destroyed our economy by creating the worst inflation crisis in history, instituting burdensome red tape and stifling American energy dominance. "President Trump has fixed the disaster that Joe Biden created by cooling inflation, signing the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowering drug prices and reshoring our manufacturing industry. The fake news won’t, so President Trump will continue to tout his economic wins to Americans." Jean-Pierre admitted the Biden administration misread the public and said her press briefings fueled much of the debate surrounding Biden's age, in addition to the economic messaging. "We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it," she conceded. TRUMP VS HISTORY: HOW PRESIDENT'S POLL NUMBERS COMPARE TO BIDEN, OBAMA, BUSH AHEAD OF MIDTERMS She also pointed to the changing media ecosystem and said a "TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump" would get more attention than her press briefings or a Cabinet official on the Sunday news programs. "The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds," Jean-Pierre wrote. "His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated. "Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now." KAROLINE LEAVITT REVEALS SHE’S ADVISED TRUMP ON WHITE HOUSE REPLACEMENT IN FINAL INTERVIEW AS PRESS SECRETARY Jean-Pierre released a book in 2025, "Independent," about her time in the White House. Ahead of its release, she revealed she was leaving the Democratic Party and registering as an Independent. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The Democratic Party had defined my life, my career," Jean-Pierre wrote. "Everything I’d done to make people’s lives better had been connected to it. The party was the vehicle that allowed me not just to have a front seat to history, working first on [Barack] Obama’s presidential campaign then in his administration, but also to make some history of my own as the first Black woman and openly queer person to ever be a White House press secretary. Never had I considered leaving the party until now."

President Trump said he was worried about North Carolina GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley’s election chances as the Senate Republican super PAC began canceling reservations in the state Friday.

“I think he’s a great man, and I am worried about him,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn en route to a campaign rally in Alabama.

“I hope he wins. He was a great leader for the whole Republican Party when I won, and he’d be a great senator,” he continued.

Trump’s comments come after the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC for Senate GOP leadership, canceled $6.5 million ad reservations in North Carolina on Friday.

Polls show Whatley trailing his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper (D).

A Catawba College and YouGov poll released this week showed Cooper with a 10-point lead over Whatley. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Democrat.”

Trump and Vice President Vance each traveled to North Carolina to campaign with Whatley last month.

articles.title: Ex-US congressman David Rivera sentenced to 10 years in prison for lobbying
articles.summary: River's ex-housemate, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, testified he had no idea about his activities.
articles.body:
A former US congressman has been sentenced to 10 years in a federal prison for money laundering and working as an undeclared foreign agent.

David Rivera, 61, who was elected as a Florida Republican, was found guilty in May after a seven-week trial heard Venezuela's state-run oil company hired his consulting firm to lobby members of Congress to help improve US relations with Venezuela.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a former housemate of Rivera, and Texas congressman Pete Sessions both testified to the court that they had no idea about his activities.

Defence lawyers had said the lobbying was for a US subsidiary of the oil company, not the Venezuelan government.

Rivera's associate, political consultant Esther Nuhfer, who was tried alongside him, was also found guilty in the case.

As a part of his sentence, Rivera, who served in Congress from 2011-13, must also forfeit his Florida properties.

Federal prosecutors in Florida said Rivera and Nuhfer engaged in a "secret political influence campaign", receiving a $50m (£37m) contract for three months of work on behalf of a US-based subsidiary of Venezuelan state oil firm PDVSA, which is also known as Citgo.

Prosecutors alleged that, in 2017 and 2018, at the behest of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's government, Rivera and Nuhfer attempted to lobby Rubio - then still a senator and former housemate of Rivera - as well as Kellyanne Conway, a former senior White House adviser.

The lobbying came during a moment of tense relations between the US and Venezuela, during President Donald Trump's first term in the White House when his administration imposed sanctions on the South American country.

Defence lawyers for Rivera and Nuhfer argued that the pair did not need to register as foreign agents because their contract was with a US-based subsidiary of a Venezuelan state company.

But Judge Melissa Damian said during Friday's sentencing: "There's no dispute this money came from the Maduro regime."

Rubio, who was not implicated in the wrongdoing, testified during the trial that he was close friends with Rivera but was unaware he was working as a lobbyist.

articles.title: Ex-GOP lawmaker sentenced to 10 years in prison
articles.summary: Former Florida Rep. David Rivera (R) was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison Friday for his undisclosed role in a multimillion-dollar lobbying campaign on behalf of the Venezuelan government under the first Trump administration. Rivera, a longtime friend and former roommate of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been in federal custody without bond…
articles.body:
Former Florida Rep. David Rivera (R) was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison Friday for his undisclosed role in a multimillion-dollar lobbying campaign on behalf of the Venezuelan government under the first Trump administration.

Rivera, a longtime friend and former roommate of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been in federal custody without bond since a Miami jury convicted him in May on charges of conspiracy to commit money laundering and other crimes connected to this $50 million lobbying scheme .

The campaign ran from 2017 to 2018 under ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro’s regime. Rivera was not serving in the House when he and his consultant, Esther Nuhfer, secretly lobbied U.S. lawmakers and members of the first Trump administration on behalf of PDV USA, the U.S. affiliate of Venezuela’s state-run oil company.

The pair was found guilty of violating the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) after a weeks-long trial, during which Rubio, Texas Rep. Pete Sessions (R) and a top Washington lobbyist testified . All asserted they were unaware of a contract between PDV USA and Rivera’s consulting company.

Prosecutors alleged in an 11-page indictment unsealed in 2022 that Venezuela’s then-foreign minister, Delcy Rodríguez, recruited Rivera to try to convince the Trump administration to ease sanctions on the country. Rodríguez has served as the acting Venezuelan president since the U.S. arrested Maduro in January.

President Trump opted not to loosen these restrictions, instead moving to sanction Maduro’s government within his first six months in the White House.

The indictment also claimed Rivera and Nuhfer signed a contract to receive a total of $50 million from the scheme — broken up into five $5 million payments and one amounting to $25 million. The pair ultimately received about $20 million after the company terminated the contract, prosecutors said.

Rivera’s attorneys argued that the defendants operated in good faith and were not required to disclose their work under FARA. The defense lawyers previously applied for a presidential pardon in June and plan to appeal this sentence, according to The Associated Press .

The Republican represented Florida’s 25th Congressional District in the House for one term from 2011 to 2013. He was fined $456,000 in 2021 following several state and federal investigations into his role in an improper campaign finance scheme.

His consultant was given a five-year prison sentence in August for her role in the illegal lobbying, the Miami Herald reported .

articles.title: Justice Alito confirms he is considering retirement
articles.summary: The conservative Supreme Court justice said in a CBS News interview that he’ll revisit the issue next year.
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has confirmed that he is considering retirement, leaving open the possibility that he could leave after next year's term and hand another nomination to President Donald Trump.

Alito said in excerpts of a CBS News interview released Friday that he thought about retiring this year and will do so again in 2027.

"It's something that I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term," the 76-year-old said in the interview scheduled to air Monday . "But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place."

Alito's interview, the first in a number of expected appearances to coincide with the release of a book about his judicial philosophy , raises the possibility that Trump, whose judicial picks shifted the Supreme Court to the right, may get an opportunity to nominate a fourth justice.

The president, who expressed regret in a recent interview about several nominees who ruled against his administration on some issues, would have a harder time getting a fourth pick through the Senate if Democrats win control in the midterms.

Alito, in the CBS interview, pushed back on concerns that the timing of his retirement and his replacement could potentially unravel his work on the bench.

"It's too hard to predict what the political situation will be and what any president might do with respect to a replacement," he said.

Alito also defended his majority opinion in June 2022 that struck down Roe v. Wade and overturned the constitutional protections for abortion that had prevailed for decades. The decision closely matched one that had leaked a month earlier .

"We didn't know it when we produced the draft that was leaked, but it required courage to go ahead with that because of the implications," he said.

He said the decision resulted in the loss of old friendships.

"That's something you have to live with," he said, adding, "It's part of the job that you're going to displease people by making decisions on controversial matters, because one side or the other is going to really dislike you because of the decisions."

articles.title: Families sue to stop Trump’s ban on medical care for trans youth
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Families sue to stop Trump’s ban on medical care for trans youth A group of four New Hampshire families are suing the Trump administration to block the implementation of a rule barring federal Medicaid dollars for gender-affirming healthcare for minors.…
articles.body:
Families sue to stop Trump’s ban on medical care for trans youth

A group of four New Hampshire families are suing the Trump administration to block the implementation of a rule barring federal Medicaid dollars for gender-affirming healthcare for minors .

Represented by GLAD Law, the National Center for LGBTQ Rights and the ACLU of New Hampshire, the families argue the rule violates existing Medicaid statute and exceeds the administration’s authority. Without being paused, the rule will take effect on Oct. 13 .

In August, the administration finalized a rule barring Medicaid from paying for what it refers to as “sex-rejecting procedures for children under 18” as well as blocking the Children’s Health Insurance Plan from paying for the same procedures for people under the age of 19.

“These families made medical decisions with their doctors, based on careful assessment of their children’s individual medical needs. On October 13, the Trump administration wants to pull the funding for their care mid-treatment, with no plan for what happens to them. We’re asking the court to act quickly so these families don’t lose the medical care that has enabled their kids to thrive,” Chris Erchull, senior staff attorney for GLAD, said in a statement.

Their complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire, argues the final rule is a result of “political directive” and not “reasoned deliberation,” noting that it preserves funding of pharmaceutical and surgical interventions for diagnoses other than gender dysphoria despite the treatments being the same.

articles.title: The shifting Senate map: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Bridget Bowman digs into a major development in the battle for the Senate. Plus, Kristen Welker examines the headwinds facing the GOP as President Donald Trump kicks off his midterm tour. — Adam Wollner The shifting Senate map By Bridget Bowman A big move today from a leading Republican super PAC underscores the increasingly tough Senate landscape the party is confronting as it tries to hang on to its majority. Senate Leadership Fund, which is aligned with Senate GOP leadership, canceled its future ad spending in the Senate race in battleground North Carolina and launched a new ad effort in deep-red Kansas. (Semafor was first to report the news.) Republicans have been pessimistic for weeks about their prospects in North Carolina, with former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper leading in recent polling and outspending former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. SLF had been heavily involved in the race: In September, it spent more than $17 million, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance also each traveled to the state last month to boost Whatley, whom Trump personally encouraged to run for retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat. “I am worried about him. I hope he wins,” Trump told reporters of Whatley today. “He’s a great man.” The GOP’s confidence is also dwindling in another swing state, Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has similarly established a clear polling and fundraising advantage over Republican Rep. Mike Collins. But one person familiar with SLF’s spending noted the group has not paused its spending in that race. Meanwhile, in solidly Republican Kansas, the race between GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton has become more competitive in the homestretch, even though the state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. So far, SLF has reserved more than $8 million in airtime in Kansas, according to AdImpact. The diversion of resources to Kansas reflects that the battle for Senate control has shifted to red states. Trump carried eight of the 10 states where SLF is spending money on ads from October through Election Day. Vance is set to travel to one of those states, Alaska, next week. (Keep reading below for more on Trump’s midterm travel). Read more → Trump broadcasts midterm anxieties as he begins a 17-state tour Analysis by Kristen Welker President Donald Trump doesn’t just want voters to pretend he’s on the ballot this midterm election, he is going to ask for their support in person as well. As NBC News reported yesterday, Trump is set to travel to 17 states for 36 events in 30 days, according to a White House official. It’s an ambitious schedule that further emphasizes what the president told a crowd in Oklahoma last night: “We’re worried.” “We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states,” Trump said, “but it’s all about 35 different contests; not states, contests. And I’m going to just about all. I’m going to Alaska.” There are a number of factors creating obstacles for Republicans heading into Election Day, including the president’s record low approval ratings on his handling of the economy, which is the No. 1 issue for voters across the board. Today, the final jobs report ahead of the midterms showed a slowing job market and wages lagging behind inflation. The job numbers, which were much lower than expected, come just as Trump is due to rally in many rural, blue-collar communities. During his Oklahoma rally, he once again promised that “if the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket and the economic success for our country like you’ve never seen before,” addressing the financial pressure voters are feeling. It’s not just the economy where Trump’s facing the headwinds — it’s immigration, too. As a candidate, he promised to oversee the “largest deportation program in American history.” But his hard-edged deportation policies have been deeply unpopular with Americans, including many of the Hispanic voters who helped him win in 2024. So while Trump tours red states to help motivate his base, one of the key factors in determining the outcome of November’s elections will be the president’s standing with Latino and independent voters. NBC News polling averages show independents’ approval of Trump’s job performance is at just 26%. And this Sunday on Meet the Press, Steve Kornacki will unveil the results of a new NBC News/Telemundo poll of Latino voters. I’ll also talk to former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel and Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., about the midterm fight ahead. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Trump visa policies weigh on Columbia journalism program as admissions pause
articles.summary: The drop in international applications shows how uncertainty over Trump’s visa policies is affecting one of the preeminent U.S. journalism institutions.
articles.body: The Trump administration’s changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, four people familiar with the matter said. The journalism school announced on Thursday it was pausing admissions to its Master of Arts offering to conduct a “critical evaluation,” without giving further details about the reasons. Jelani Cobb, the journalism school’s dean, said admissions to its Master of Arts program would pause for one year while the school reworked a degree created in 2005, when the “journalism marketplace looked different.” “The dynamics of visas and all those other kinds of things were part of the consideration,” Cobb told Reuters. Additionally, the department needs time to think through changes to the program, he added. The connection between the admissions pause and U.S. visa policies has not been previously reported, nor has the length of the admissions pause. The drop in international applications shows how uncertainty over President Donald Trump’s visa policies is affecting one of the preeminent U.S. journalism institutions, which also administers the profession’s highest U.S. honor, the Pulitzer Prize. The people did not disclose the exact size of the drop in applications. Last year, the Trump administration temporarily halted new student-visa appointments, then resumed them with expanded screening of applicants’ online activity, saying the checks were needed to identify potential threats to U.S. national security. Columbia was among the universities targeted by his administration over pro-Palestinian campus protests in 2024. Last year, it agreed to pay over $200 million to settle federal investigations and regain most of its suspended federal funding. A new rule this year also sought to limit how long foreign students and journalists could stay in the U.S. without seeking extensions, but a federal judge blocked it before it took effect last month, calling its rationale “exceptionally weak.” Visa difficulties and immigration policy uncertainty have deterred prospective Columbia journalism students from abroad, the four people said, requesting anonymity to discuss its admissions. International students make up roughly half of the M.A. program’s enrollment, the people said. Kaushik Raj, an Indian journalist admitted to Columbia’s separate M.S. program in data journalism, was denied a U.S. student visa last year, the Intercept reported. His rejection letter said he had not shown sufficient ties to India to establish he would return after his studies, according to the report. Geared toward mid-career journalists seeking expertise in subjects such as politics, business and science, the M.A. program is smaller than the Master of Science program aimed at students with less journalism experience. The school is not pausing the M.S. program. Lower enrollment has prompted changes to the M.A. program, including the combination of science and politics seminars in the 2024-25 academic year, two of the people familiar with the matter said. On Thursday, the school also announced a two-year, part-time online M.S. program. The move could allow Columbia to enroll international students without visas, but Cobb said it was unrelated to the M.A. admissions pause because the programs serve different students. The M.A. pause comes as news organizations grapple with AI’s potential to reshape how stories are produced and found, while falling search traffic piles pressure on their business. Last year, at least 3,434 journalism jobs were cut in the U.K. and U.S., according to a Press Gazette tracker. The BBC and CBS News have announced layoffs this year. Some journalists took to social media on Thursday to criticize the M.A. program as too short and too expensive. The course spans nine months and Columbia estimates the cost of attendance at $120,000 before financial aid. The yearlong M.S. in Data Journalism costs about $180,000. Two of the people familiar with the matter said the financial assistance made tuition less of a deterrent because most students receive financial aid. About 80% of the students receive financial aid, including grants, loans, or scholarships from institutional, federal and private funds, according to its website. Cobb said the journalism school wants to create a new fundraising strategy for the M.A. program and is considering starting a part-time version.

Major economies will release fuel, including diesel, from their stockpiles as prices have skyrocketed in recent weeks.

The Group of Seven (G7), which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S., said in a statement Friday that it would “begin immediately” releasing 100 million barrels of fuel over the next four months.

This is expected to include a “frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners” the group said.

In addition, the countries said they will “coordinate maintenance schedules” of their refineries that process oil into fuels including gasoline and diesel, to “prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible.”

“We also encourage engagement with countries holding significant refining capacities to boost global production of refined products, particularly diesel, in light of ongoing market pressures in this segment,” the countries said.

Their statement did not specify which countries the releases would come form.

articles.body:
Justice Samuel Alito said his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022 alongside the Supreme Court’s six conservative justices took “courage.”

In a preview for his interview with CBS News, Alito was asked if there was a particular decision that took courage.

“Well, the leading example is Dobbs [v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization]. I think that required courage by all of the justices in the majority,” he said. “We didn’t know it at the time. We didn’t know it when we produced the draft that was leaked, but it required courage to go ahead with that because of the implications.”

“There are others. I mean, there are cases that have resulted in the loss of old friendships; that’s something that you have to live with,” Alito continued.

When asked if part of the job of a Supreme Court justice is to lose friends, receive death threats or wear a bulletproof vest, he responded, “It’s part of the job that you’re going to displease people by making decisions on controversial matters because one side or the other is going to really dislike you because of the decisions.”

“The physical threats and the harassment represent something new in our society and something that’s quite disturbing, and I think it’s a danger,” Alito concluded.

More than four years ago, the Supreme Court eliminated the nearly 50-year-old constitutional right to abortion and handed states authority to drastically limit or ban the procedure.

Alito wrote in the majority opinion — which was leaked a month before it was unveiled — “Roe was egregiously wrong from the start,” adding that its precedent “had damaging consequences.”

The decision drew public outcry with protests outside the Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said at the time the decision marked “one of the darkest days our country has ever seen.”

An NBC poll from 2023 found 53 percent of Americans strongly disapprove of Roe v. Wade’s overturn.

articles.title: Alito: ‘I thought about’ retiring at end of last term
articles.summary: Justice Samuel Alito said he “thought about” retiring from the Supreme Court at the end of his last term following speculation about his potential retirement this year. In an interview with CBS News, chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford asked Alito if he considered retiring in the face of “some pretty intense pressure from Republicans” who…
articles.body:
Justice Samuel Alito said he “thought about” retiring from the Supreme Court at the end of his last term following speculation about his potential retirement this year.

In an interview with CBS News , chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford asked Alito if he considered retiring in the face of “some pretty intense pressure from Republicans” who wanted to confirm his replacement while the GOP maintained control of the Senate.

“I thought about it,” Alito said. “Well, it’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term.”

“But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place. So that is basically it,” he continued.

Alito added that he would “have to” continue to think about retirement every year.

Crawford also asked whether his potential future retirement would “risk undoing all the work that you have done here at the court,” drawing a comparison to the late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

“I think it’s too hard to predict. It’s too hard to predict, for anybody, particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now, and so forth,” Alito said. “And it’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be, and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”

Alito, 76, has been on the Supreme Court for a little over two decades after President George W. Bush nominated him for the role, and is the court’s second-oldest justice, behind Justice Clarence Thomas, 78.

He is part of the court’s conservative bloc, alongside Justices John Roberts, Clarence Thomas, Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch.

He shut down any notion of his retirement in August, telling the Wall Street Journal , “obviously I’m here for another term.”

Alito’s remarks followed NPR erroneously reporting that he had announced his retirement on the final opinion day of the court’s term. The report was retracted and NPR journalist Nina Totenberg apologized to Alito in a letter.
